lesson_title: Sorting the Washing: Collecting and Summarising Data
hook_text: The average wait was 55 minutes. The typical wait was 45. Both are true — and only one of them is honest.
clip_script: A clinic. Fifteen patients. Somebody wrote down how long each one waited, and the list came back jumbled — useless. So do what you do with washing: sort it first. Twenty, twenty-five, twenty-five, thirty... all the way up to a hundred and forty. Now the story shows itself — a crowd of shortish waits, and three that ran away. Share all the minutes out equally and you get an average of 55 minutes. But line everyone up shortest to longest and the person standing dead in the middle waited only 45. Why the gap? Because three patients waited 90, 120 and 140 minutes, and those long waits drag the average up — the same way one uncle with a big salary lifts the "average income" of a family where everybody else is struggling. The middle number doesn't get dragged. So when somebody quotes you an average, ask what the middle is. If they're far apart, somebody at the edges is doing the pulling — and that's usually the real story.
visual_style: A clinic corridor, then fifteen numbered cards shuffling themselves into a neat ascending line; three cards at the far end glowing red as an average marker slides toward them while a median marker stays put.
mood: Curious and quietly revealing — the satisfaction of seeing a hidden story surface.
pacing: Unhurried sorting rhythm, a beat of stillness at the two numbers, sharp punch on the closing warning.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and learn which average is telling you the truth.
